title: Consent for appendicectomy: a 38-year-old man on the surgical ward
desc: This station involves a focused pre-operative history and examination of a 38-year-old carpenter admitted with right iliac fossa pain and booked for theatre tomorrow. The candidate then interprets his observations, admission bloods and CT report, recognises acute uncomplicated appendicitis and plans his preparation for theatre. They then explain the operation to him (nature, benefits, risks, alternatives, the consequences of no treatment and the day itself) to gain informed consent, and safety-net.
focus: Pre-operative assessment and informed consent for laparoscopic appendicectomy (NBARCO)
stem:
You are the intern on the general surgical team at a metropolitan hospital. Michael Green, a 38-year-old man, was admitted through the Emergency Department last night with abdominal pain and nausea. He had a CT scan before coming to the ward. He was expected to have his operation today but missed the list because of emergency theatre demand, and he is now on tomorrow morning's emergency theatre list.

Your registrar has asked you to assess Michael before his operation and to take his consent for the procedure. You have completed your hospital's consent training for appendicectomy, and your registrar is available by phone.
tasks: Take a focused pre-operative history from Michael, including what he understands about why he is here, and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Michael's observations, admission blood tests and CT report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach, including explaining the operation to Michael and seeking his consent, and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Michael Green, a 38-year-old self-employed carpenter. You are lying in bed on the surgical ward with a cannula in your left arm (nothing is running through it at the moment). Painkillers have made you comfortable now. You are a bit tired, friendly and keen to understand what is going on. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining. If the candidate uses medical words (for example "laparoscopic" or "peritonitis") without explaining them, ask: "Sorry, what does that mean?"

Opening line: "I came in because of this pain in my stomach. It started off okay, kind of achy, then got a lot worse over the day and moved down near my right hip. The last doctor said they think I've got appendicitis and I'm having surgery, but nobody's said anything more than that."

The pain (give only when asked):

  • It started yesterday morning, about 7 am, as a dull ache around your belly button.
  • By the afternoon it was sharp and much worse and had moved down to the right side, near your hip. Walking, and the bumps in the car on the way in, made it worse.
  • At its worst it was 8 out of 10. If asked how it is now: "The pain isn't too bad at the moment. They gave me some painkillers which helped." About 3 out of 10.
  • You have never had anything like it before.

Other symptoms (only if asked):

  • You have felt sick since yesterday and vomited once yesterday afternoon. You have not felt like eating.
  • You felt hot and sweaty last night. No shakes or shivers.
  • Your bowels opened normally yesterday morning but not since. No diarrhoea, no blood in your poo.
  • No weight loss. No previous bouts of diarrhoea or tummy pain.
  • No pain or burning when passing urine, no blood in your urine, no pain in your back or loin.

Past medical and anaesthetic history:

  • No medical problems. You have never been in hospital before.
  • Only if asked about operations or anaesthetics: you had your wisdom teeth out under a general anaesthetic at 21. "I felt a bit sick afterwards but otherwise fine."
  • No one in your family has had a problem with an anaesthetic.
  • No bleeding problems, no easy bruising, no clots in the legs or lungs.
  • No heartburn. Your partner says you snore "a little". No chest pain or breathlessness. You play touch football every week and climb ladders all day.
  • You last ate toast for breakfast yesterday and have had only sips of water since.
  • Teeth: all your own, no caps or loose teeth.

Medications: none. No blood thinners, no anti-inflammatories, no vitamins or supplements.

Allergies: none to medicines (including antibiotics), latex, plasters or foods.

Social history:

  • You are a self-employed carpenter, and your work involves heavy lifting.
  • You live with your partner Sarah and your two children, aged 6 and 9. Sarah can drive you home and help out.
  • You have never smoked. Alcohol, only if asked how much: "a few beers on the weekend", about 4 to 6 standard drinks a week. No recreational drugs.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: "I think the appendix is infected and has to come out, but I don't really know what the appendix even is."
  • Concerns: how long you will be off work, because you are self-employed, and whether you will have a big scar.
  • Expectation: you want someone to explain properly what is going to happen, then get it done.

Question to raise once in Part 1: "Will you be able to explain what they're actually going to do to me?" Accept it if the candidate says they will explain once they have finished the history and examination.

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: comfortable lying still in bed, alert, not pale or jaundiced. Cannula in the left forearm, site clean. Weight 82 kg, height 180 cm.
  • Observations (14:00): temperature 37.5 °C, HR 92 regular, BP 126/78, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, capillary BGL 5.4 mmol/L, pain 3/10.
  • Hydration: mucous membranes slightly dry, capillary refill 2 seconds.
  • Airway: good mouth opening, full neck movement, own teeth with none loose, Mallampati class 1.
  • Heart and chest: heart sounds dual, no murmurs. Chest clear.
  • Abdomen, inspection: not distended, no scars, moves with breathing.
  • Abdomen, palpation: tender in the right iliac fossa, worst at McBurney's point, with mild voluntary guarding there. Percussion tenderness in the right iliac fossa only. Rovsing's sign positive. The rest of the abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no rigidity. No palpable mass. No hepatosplenomegaly. Murphy's sign negative.
  • Bowel sounds: present, normal.
  • Renal angles: non-tender. Hernial orifices: clear.
  • Calves: soft and non-tender.
  • Genital or rectal examination: if offered, the examiner says it is not needed today.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self as the surgical intern, and confirms Michael's identity (full name, date of birth, wristband) before the consent discussion.
Uses plain language or explains terms, and checks he is alert enough (not drowsy from opioids) to make a decision.
check.d: Award for plain language (or explaining any terms used) plus the alertness check.

check.x: History
Asks what he understands about his condition and the plan, and what he has been told (likely appendicitis and surgery, nothing more), before giving information.
Takes a brief history of the presenting illness:

kids.x: Onset and migration: a dull periumbilical ache from yesterday morning that became sharp and moved to the right iliac fossa, worse with movement.
Current pain: about 3/10 after analgesia (8/10 at worst).
Associated symptoms: nausea, one vomit, anorexia, felt feverish without rigors; bowel and urinary symptoms (none).
kids.d: Award for at least three of: nausea/vomiting, anorexia, fever or rigors, bowel symptoms, urinary symptoms.

check.x: Takes a pre-anaesthetic history:

kids.x: Previous operations and anaesthetics and any problems with them: wisdom teeth under general anaesthetic, nausea afterwards.
Family history of anaesthetic problems (for example malignant hyperthermia, or prolonged paralysis after an anaesthetic).
Bleeding or clotting history, reflux, snoring or sleep apnoea, exercise tolerance, and when he last ate and drank.
kids.d: Award for at least three of these.

check.x: Asks about medications, including blood thinners, anti-inflammatories and supplements (none), and allergies, including medicines, antibiotics and latex (none).

Takes the past medical and social history: no medical problems; never smoked; quantifies alcohol (4 to 6 standard drinks a week); no drugs; self-employed carpenter; lives with his partner and two children, and someone can take him home.
check.d: Award for past history plus smoking, alcohol quantified, and work or home support.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: unsure what the appendix is, worried about time off work and the scar, wants a proper explanation; acknowledges his worry about time off work and says recovery will be covered with the operation.
check.d: Credit telling him, at any point in Part 1 or Part 2, that he will be back to heavy work after a few weeks (no heavy lifting for about 2 to 6 weeks).

check.x: Examination
Asks for the observations and notes no signs of sepsis or organ dysfunction (T 37.5 °C, HR 92, normal BP and SpO2, alert).
Assesses hydration (slightly dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 2 seconds).
Examines the abdomen:

kids.x: Inspects (no distension or scars) and palpates gently, starting away from the pain.
Finds localised right iliac fossa tenderness at McBurney's point with mild guarding and percussion tenderness, and states there is no generalised peritonism or rigidity (no sign of perforation).
Checks for a mass, bowel sounds, Rovsing's sign, renal angles and hernial orifices.

check.x: Performs a pre-operative check of the heart, chest and airway (mouth opening, teeth, neck movement), and checks the calves.
check.d: Award for heart and chest plus the airway.

check.x: Interpretation

Interprets the observations: all values sit in the white area of the chart and are stable from 14:00 to 18:00, with no new fever or rising heart rate; no call criteria are met. Notes that no antibiotics have been given.
check.d: Accept a candidate who notes he meets SIRS criteria but has no organ dysfunction.

check.x: Interprets the bloods: raised WCC (13.8) with neutrophilia (11.2) and a CRP of 48 fit acute inflammation; haemoglobin, platelets, renal function, LFTs and lipase are normal; the group and screen is done (O Rh(D) positive, antibody screen negative), so blood can be provided if needed.
check.d: Award for the inflammatory markers, at least two of the normal results, and the group and screen.

check.x: Interprets the CT: a dilated (11 mm), thick-walled, enhancing appendix with periappendiceal fat stranding; no appendicolith, free gas, abscess or collection; normal terminal ileum and no urinary calculi. This is acute uncomplicated appendicitis without perforation.
States the diagnosis as acute uncomplicated appendicitis and justifies it from the migratory pain, nausea and anorexia, localised right iliac fossa signs, inflammatory markers and CT.

Gives at least three differentials, each with a feature for or against (for example perforated appendicitis or abscess, terminal ileal Crohn's disease, right ureteric colic, right-sided diverticulitis).
check.d: Award for three differentials with a feature for or against each.

check.x: Management

Gives a structured ISBAR handover to the registrar that includes the results and ends with a clear recommendation: confirms timing because he will be over 24 hours from diagnosis (tonight's emergency list if possible, otherwise first on the morning list), and the overnight plan.
check.d: Credit either timing request (tonight's list, or first on the morning list) as long as the candidate asks the registrar to confirm it.

check.x: Plans his preparation for theatre:

kids.x: Fasting as the anaesthetist instructs (ANZCA PG07): no food for at least 6 hours before surgery, clear fluids as the anaesthetist allows, with IV maintenance fluids while he is not eating or drinking.
kids.d: Accept 'nil by mouth from midnight' as long as the candidate mentions the anaesthetic team's instructions.

kids.x: Regular paracetamol with an opioid as needed, and an antiemetic.

Starts or continues IV antibiotics per eTG because surgery is delayed overnight, and makes sure prophylaxis (cefazolin 2 g plus metronidazole 500 mg IV) is given within 60 minutes before incision unless the antibiotics he is already on cover it.
kids.d: Accept any eTG-concordant regimen; doses are not needed for the mark.

kids.x: VTE risk assessment and prophylaxis per local protocol.

Confirms the theatre booking and that the group and hold will still be valid at the time of surgery, and informs the anaesthetist, including his history of nausea after anaesthetic, for pre-anaesthetic review.

check.x: In plain words explains keyhole removal of the infected appendix under general anaesthetic, and that without it, it could burst, causing an abscess or peritonitis that can be life-threatening.
check.d: Explaining what the appendix is is creditable but not required. One sentence is enough: a keyhole operation under general anaesthetic to take out the infected appendix through small cuts, so it does not burst.

check.x: States the key material risks (bleeding, infection in the wound or inside the abdomen, injury to nearby organs, conversion to open, anaesthetic risks) and puts them in context.
check.d: Award for at least three of the five risks plus a statement that serious complications are uncommon. A list of three in one sentence is enough.

check.x: Answers his question about antibiotics alone: most settle at first, but about 1 in 3 need surgery later; surgery is recommended; the choice is his.
check.d: The trial figures (APPAC 27% at 1 year; CODA 29% by 90 days) are not required.

check.x: Asks explicitly whether he agrees to go ahead, tells him he can change his mind, and mentions the consent form naming the procedure.
check.d: Award for explicitly asking whether he agrees plus telling him he can change his mind; mentioning the consent form is creditable but not required.

check.x: Safety netting
Tells him to press the call bell straight away tonight, rather than waiting for the morning, for at least two of: pain much worse or spreading, fever or shakes, repeated vomiting, feeling faint.
check.d: Award for the call bell straight away plus at least two red flags in plain words.

check.x: Plans 4-hourly observations overnight and asks for escalation to the surgical team for a new fever, rising heart rate, falling BP or worsening pain (possible perforation).

part2.lead: It is now early evening. Here are Michael's observations from this afternoon, his admission blood tests and the report of the CT scan he had in the Emergency Department last night.
part2.patient:
Ask this once while the candidate explains the operation:

  • "My mate had appendicitis and just took antibiotics. Can't I just do that instead?"

If the explanation is clear and your question is answered, say you are happy to go ahead and sign the form. If the candidate does not ask whether you agree, do not offer to sign. If the candidate uses jargon without explaining it, ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Room air throughout. Only regular paracetamol is charted; no IV antibiotics have been started since he arrived (the ED expected him to go to theatre today).
handover.model:
• Read: RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, BP 126/78 then 124/76, HR 92 then 86, temperature 37.5 then 37.4 °C, alert, pain 3 then 2/10. Every value sits in the white area of the NSW adult chart. There are no yellow or red zone criteria, so no clinical review or rapid response is triggered.
  • For Michael: haemodynamically stable with no fever or developing tachycardia, so no sign of perforation or sepsis. He has had no antibiotics.
  • What it changes: he is stable now, but by tomorrow morning he will be beyond the 24-hour delay WSES accepts, so flag the timing to the registrar: tonight's emergency list if possible, otherwise first on the morning list. Because surgery is delayed, start empirical IV antibiotics per eTG now. Continue 4-hourly observations. A new fever, a rising heart rate, a falling BP or worsening pain would need urgent registrar review for possible perforation.

handover.label: Admission blood tests
handover.result: Collected in the Emergency Department at 21:15 last night.
handover.model:
• Read: WCC 13.8 with neutrophils 11.2 (neutrophilia) and a CRP of 48: an acute inflammatory response. Haemoglobin and platelets normal. Electrolytes, urea and creatinine normal. Bilirubin, liver enzymes and lipase normal. Group O Rh(D) positive with a negative antibody screen.
  • For Michael: the markers fit acute appendicitis. They are not specific and do not by themselves show perforation. Normal lipase and LFTs argue against pancreatitis and biliary disease. Normal renal function means the IV contrast was safe and no dose changes are needed.
  • What it changes: his bloods do not stop him going to theatre. The group and screen means blood can be provided quickly if there is unexpected bleeding; check the sample is still valid for the time of surgery under local policy.

labs.title: Liver function tests, lipase and CRP
Blood group and antibody screen (group and hold)

handover.label: CT abdomen and pelvis
handover.result:
Examination: CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast (portal venous phase). No oral contrast.

Clinical details: 38-year-old man with periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa, nausea, and right iliac fossa tenderness. ?Appendicitis.

Comparison: none.

Findings:

  • Appendix: arises normally from the caecum and lies in the right iliac fossa. Dilated to 11 mm with a thickened, enhancing wall and surrounding fat stranding. No appendicolith. The wall is intact, with no extraluminal gas.
  • Peritoneum: no free gas. No abscess or drainable collection. A trace of fluid next to the appendix only.
  • Bowel: caecum and terminal ileum normal, with no wall thickening. No diverticula in the right colon. No bowel obstruction.
  • Lymph nodes: a few small reactive mesenteric nodes in the right iliac fossa, none enlarged.
  • Solid organs: liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen and adrenals normal.
  • Urinary tract: kidneys enhance normally, no hydronephrosis, no urinary tract calculi. Bladder normal.
  • Bones and lung bases: unremarkable.

Conclusion: acute appendicitis with no CT evidence of perforation, abscess or appendicolith.
handover.model:
• Read: a dilated (11 mm), thick-walled, enhancing appendix with periappendiceal fat stranding; no appendicolith, free gas, abscess or collection. Normal terminal ileum and caecum, no right-sided diverticula, no urinary calculi or hydronephrosis, and a normal gallbladder and pancreas.
  • For Michael: confirms acute uncomplicated appendicitis. The negative findings argue against perforation, Crohn's disease of the terminal ileum, caecal diverticulitis and a ureteric stone.
  • What it changes: he is suitable for laparoscopic appendicectomy on the next list. Because the appendicitis is uncomplicated and there is no appendicolith, antibiotics alone are a reasonable alternative to discuss, though with a real risk of recurrence.

ask: You are now calling the general surgical registrar. Please give an ISBAR handover of Michael Green, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Michael now, here on the surgical ward, as you prepare him for theatre tomorrow.
Please explain to Michael the operation he is having tomorrow, including its benefits, risks and alternatives, seek his consent, and tell him what to look out for tonight.
expect:
• Identify: self, surgical intern, ward; Michael Green, 38.
  • Situation: acute uncomplicated appendicitis confirmed on CT; missed today's list, now on tomorrow morning's list; stable.
  • Background: pain since yesterday morning migrating to the RIF, nausea and anorexia; well, no medicines or allergies; nausea after a previous GA.
  • Assessment: localised RIF peritonism only; obs stable in the white zone; WCC 13.8, CRP 48, otherwise normal bloods, G&S done; CT uncomplicated appendicitis, no perforation or collection; no antibiotics yet.
  • Recommendation: he will be over 24 hours from diagnosis: can he go tonight, or else first on the morning list? I will start IV antibiotics per eTG now; please review if he deteriorates.

Most likely: acute uncomplicated appendicitis. Periumbilical pain migrating to the RIF, nausea and anorexia, McBurney's point tenderness with guarding, neutrophilia and a raised CRP, and an inflamed appendix on CT without perforation.

  • Perforated appendicitis or appendiceal abscess: for: more than 30 hours of symptoms, raised CRP. Against: no generalised peritonism, stable obs, no free gas or collection on CT.
  • Terminal ileal Crohn's disease: for: RIF pain and raised inflammatory markers. Against: no previous bowel symptoms or weight loss, normal terminal ileum on CT.
  • Right ureteric colic: for: acute right-sided pain with vomiting. Against: no loin pain or urinary symptoms, no calculi or hydronephrosis.
  • Right-sided diverticulitis: for: RIF pain and raised inflammatory markers. Against: no diverticula on CT.

1. Fasting as the anaesthetist instructs (ANZCA PG07): no food for at least 6 hours before surgery, clear fluids as allowed, with IV maintenance fluids while he is not eating or drinking (he is mildly dry).
  2. Analgesia: regular paracetamol 1 g 6-hourly (maximum 4 g a day), an opioid as needed (for example oxycodone 5 mg), and an antiemetic (for example ondansetron 4 mg) (doses not required for the mark).
  3. Antibiotics: none given yet and surgery is delayed overnight, so start empirical IV antibiotics per eTG; make sure prophylaxis (cefazolin 2 g plus metronidazole 500 mg IV) is given within 60 minutes before incision unless his current antibiotics cover it (doses not required for the mark).
  4. VTE: risk assessment, then mechanical and/or pharmacological prophylaxis per local protocol.
  5. Theatre: confirm timing with the registrar (tonight's emergency list if possible, otherwise first on the morning list), confirm the group and hold will still be valid at the time of surgery, inform the anaesthetist (including previous post-anaesthetic nausea), complete the consent.
  6. Observations 4-hourly; escalate for fever, tachycardia, hypotension or worsening pain.

• Nature and benefit: keyhole removal of the inflamed appendix under general anaesthetic (explaining what the appendix is is optional); without it, it could burst, causing an abscess or peritonitis that can be life-threatening.
  • Risks: at least three of: bleeding, infection, injury to nearby organs, conversion to open, anaesthetic risks; serious complications uncommon.
  • Recovery (credited anywhere): back to heavy work after a few weeks.
  • Alternative: antibiotics alone: most settle at first, but about 1 in 3 need surgery later; surgery is recommended; his choice.
  • Agreement: asks explicitly whether he agrees; he can change his mind (the consent form is a bonus).
  • Tonight: press the call bell straight away, not waiting for the morning, for worsening or spreading pain, fever or shakes, repeated vomiting or feeling faint.

ddx.for: Periumbilical pain migrating to the right iliac fossa with nausea and anorexia, McBurney's point tenderness with guarding, WCC 13.8 and CRP 48, and an 11 mm inflamed appendix on CT.
More than 30 hours of symptoms, felt feverish overnight, and a raised CRP.
ddx.against: Localised signs without generalised peritonism, stable observations, and no free gas, abscess or collection on CT.

ddx.for: Right iliac fossa pain with raised inflammatory markers in a young adult.
ddx.against: No previous diarrhoea, weight loss or blood in the stool, and a normal terminal ileum on CT.

ddx.for: Acute right-sided abdominal pain with vomiting.
ddx.against: No loin-to-groin pain or urinary symptoms, non-tender renal angles, and no calculi or hydronephrosis on CT.

ddx.for: Right iliac fossa pain, tenderness and raised inflammatory markers.
ddx.against: No diverticula in the right colon, and the inflammation is centred on the appendix on CT.

guide:
In Part 1, give examination findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. The observation chart shows the 14:00 set; give it when the candidate asks for observations. If the candidate asks for results in Part 1, say they will come in Part 2. If the candidate starts explaining the operation in Part 1, Michael can say "Can you go through all that once you've finished checking me over?" Credit any consent items given in Part 1 all the same.

In Part 2, hand over all three results and ask the four questions in order. Allow about 90 seconds for each of the four questions. The consent question is marked on these items only: nature and benefit (including what happens without treatment), at least three risks in context, the antibiotic alternative, explicit agreement with the right to change his mind (the consent form is a bonus), and red flags tonight with the call bell. Consent items already covered in Part 1 earn the marks; the candidate need not repeat them. The time off heavy work is credited wherever it comes. In question 4, credit brief plain-language statements; a full consent discussion is not expected in the time. Fluids, the anaesthetist and consent are credited from question 3, not the ISBAR. During question 4 the candidate speaks to Michael directly, and Michael asks his question once. Michael agrees and signs only if he is asked explicitly for his consent.

A high-performing candidate starts by finding out what Michael already knows and takes a tidy pre-anaesthetic history (previous anaesthetics, family anaesthetic problems, medicines, allergies, bleeding, fasting). They examine for localised versus generalised peritonism. In Part 2 they read the CT as uncomplicated appendicitis, notice he has had no antibiotics while surgery is delayed beyond 24 hours, flag the timing to the registrar and give a sensible ward plan. They then work through NBARCO in plain language: what the appendix is, the keyhole operation, the benefit, the key risks in context, antibiotics as an honest alternative, what happens if nothing is done, and the recovery. They confirm he agrees, remind him he can change his mind, mention the consent form and tell him what to watch for tonight.

A borderline candidate starts reciting a script without checking his understanding, or uses jargon. They may list risks without context or leave out serious ones, dismiss or overstate the antibiotic option, forget the family anaesthetic history or allergies, or never ask whether he agrees to go ahead.
explain:
Diagnosis

Michael has acute uncomplicated appendicitis. Periumbilical pain that moves to the right iliac fossa is the classic story. Early stretching of the appendix is felt as poorly localised visceral (midgut) pain, and the pain localises once the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed. Nausea, anorexia, McBurney's point tenderness with guarding and a positive Rovsing's sign support the diagnosis, and the CT confirms it. Appendicitis usually follows blockage of the lumen, by a faecolith or lymphoid hyperplasia, though often no cause is found. Mucus builds up and bacteria multiply, and the wall becomes inflamed, then ischaemic, and eventually perforates.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: every value is in the white area of the NSW adult chart and stable. There is no sign of sepsis or perforation, so no clinical review or rapid response is triggered, but the delay to surgery still needs flagging to the registrar (see Timing below). The note that only paracetamol is charted tells you he has had no antibiotics.
  • Bloods: neutrophilia and a raised CRP fit acute inflammation but are not specific. Normal lipase and LFTs argue against pancreatitis and biliary disease. Normal renal function matters because he had IV contrast and will have IV medicines. A group and screen (group and hold) means blood can be issued quickly if needed.
  • CT: a dilated, thick-walled, enhancing appendix with fat stranding is acute appendicitis. No free gas, abscess, collection or appendicolith makes it uncomplicated. The normal terminal ileum, right colon and urinary tract argue against Crohn's disease, caecal diverticulitis and a ureteric stone.

Differentials that matter

The one not to miss is complicated appendicitis (perforation, abscess or peritonitis). It presents with generalised peritonism, fever, tachycardia or a collection on imaging, and it changes the urgency and the operation. Terminal ileal Crohn's disease, right ureteric colic and right-sided diverticulitis are reasonable alternatives that the history and the CT argue against. The appendix is always sent for histology, because an unexpected appendiceal tumour is occasionally found.

Preparing for theatre

  • Timing: WSES accepts a short delay (up to about 24 hours) for uncomplicated appendicitis. Michael missed today's list, so his operation will be about 34 hours after diagnosis (and about 49 hours from symptom onset). This is beyond the 24-hour window, so flag it to the registrar: ask whether he can go on tonight's emergency list; if not, he should be first on the morning list with empirical IV antibiotics started now.
  • Fasting: as the anaesthetist instructs (ANZCA PG07): no food for at least 6 hours before surgery and clear fluids as the anaesthetist allows, rather than a blanket "nil by mouth from midnight". He has eaten nothing since yesterday's breakfast and is mildly dry, so give IV maintenance fluids while he is not eating or drinking.
  • Analgesia: regular paracetamol, an opioid as needed and an antiemetic. Analgesia does not mask the signs of an acute abdomen.
  • Antibiotics: eTG advises that surgical prophylaxis alone is enough when appendicectomy is done promptly, but that empirical IV treatment is needed when surgery is delayed. Michael has had no antibiotics and his surgery is delayed overnight, so start the eTG empirical regimen for appendicitis now (follow eTG and local protocol for the drugs and doses). Make sure prophylaxis (cefazolin 2 g plus metronidazole 500 mg IV) is given within 60 minutes before incision unless the antibiotics he is already on cover it.
  • Other: VTE risk assessment and prophylaxis; FBE, UEC and a valid group and hold; pre-anaesthetic review (tell the anaesthetist about his nausea after his last anaesthetic); a confirmed theatre booking.

Informed consent

Valid consent needs three things:

  • Capacity: he can understand, retain and weigh the information and communicate a decision. Check he is not drowsy from opioids.
  • Enough information.
  • Voluntariness.

Consent must also cover the specific procedure. Under Rogers v Whitaker (High Court of Australia, 1992), a doctor must warn of material risks: risks a reasonable person in the patient's position would think significant, or that the doctor knows or should know this patient would think significant. For a carpenter, recovery time and lifting restrictions are material. Begin by asking what he knows, use plain language and a picture, and give information in chunks. Local policy decides who may take consent. Usually it is someone who can perform the procedure or has been trained to consent for it, so if you are unsure, involve the registrar. A useful structure is NBARCO:

  • Nature: what the appendix and appendicitis are; laparoscopic appendicectomy through about three small cuts under general anaesthetic, with possible conversion to open surgery if the appendix cannot be found or safely removed.
  • Benefits: removes the infection and prevents perforation, abscess and peritonitis. Keyhole surgery means a shorter stay and a quicker recovery.
  • Alternatives: antibiotics alone for selected uncomplicated cases (WSES). In trials such as APPAC and CODA, most patients avoid surgery at first, but about 3 in 10 need appendicectomy within the first year (APPAC 27% at 1 year; CODA 29% by 90 days), and more over 5 years. Antibiotics fail more often when there is an appendicolith. Surgery remains the standard treatment, and the decision is shared.
  • Risks: the key ones for the consent discussion are bleeding, infection (wound or intra-abdominal collection), injury to nearby organs, conversion to open, and anaesthetic risks including allergy and nausea. Less common or longer-term risks include stump appendicitis (inflammation in the small piece of appendix left behind), adhesional bowel obstruction, incisional or port-site hernia, and chronic pain. Put them in context: serious complications are uncommon.
  • Consequences of no treatment: perforation, abscess and peritonitis.
  • On the day and opting out: fasting as the anaesthetist instructs, 1 to 2 days in hospital, and a return to activity with no heavy lifting for about 2 to 6 weeks as the surgeon advises. He can ask questions and change his mind at any time without it affecting his care.

Then confirm he understands, invite his questions, ask explicitly whether he agrees, complete the form with the procedure written in full and both signatures, and document the discussion in the notes.

Safety netting and follow-up

Tonight, before surgery, he should press the call bell and tell the nurse at once about worsening or spreading pain, fever or rigors, repeated vomiting or feeling faint, which may mean perforation. At discharge (not part of tonight's consent discussion), he should be told to go to the ED for fever, worsening pain, a red, hot or discharging wound, repeated vomiting, a swollen abdomen or not passing wind or stools. These suggest a collection, wound infection, ileus or obstruction. The discharge summary goes to the GP, with a wound check at about 1 to 2 weeks and the histology result followed up.
points: Classic appendicitis begins as vague periumbilical pain that localises to the right iliac fossa as the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed, with nausea and anorexia.

Before taking consent, find out what the patient already knows and check capacity (including drowsiness from opioids). Take a pre-anaesthetic history: previous anaesthetics, family anaesthetic problems, medicines, allergies, bleeding and fasting.
Structure consent with NBARCO: Nature, Benefits, Alternatives, Risks, Consequences of no treatment, and On the day/opting out. Use plain language and a picture.

Material risks (Rogers v Whitaker) are the ones this patient would think significant. Include bleeding, infection, organ injury, conversion to open surgery and anaesthetic risks, and for a manual worker, the time off heavy lifting.

Antibiotics alone are an option for uncomplicated appendicitis, but about 3 in 10 patients need appendicectomy within the first year (APPAC 27% at 1 year; CODA 29% by 90 days), and more over 5 years; surgery remains the standard treatment.

Preparing for theatre means fasting as the anaesthetist instructs (ANZCA PG07) with IV fluids, analgesia and an antiemetic, empirical IV antibiotics per eTG when surgery is delayed (with prophylaxis within 60 minutes before incision), VTE prophylaxis, a group and hold, anaesthetic review and a signed consent form that names the procedure. A delay beyond about 24 hours from diagnosis should be flagged to the registrar.
